issues.issue: The grant of the right to transport oil and gas "from the subject and other lands" across the leasehold, surviving the term, conflicts with paragraph 25 (transport from other lands not to be asserted unless the lands are pooled) and Addendum paragraph 20 (no right to transport foreign gas across the premises). A court would have to choose between them.

The term continues so long as gas is "produced or capable of being produced ... in paying quantities, in the judgment of the Lessee"; "paying quantities" is undefined and the Lessee's subjective judgment as the yardstick is open to competing readings.

The clause extends the term "as provided in Paragraph 7 following," yet Paragraph 7 concerns adequacy of consideration and drilling discretion, not the term; the shut-in provision is Paragraph 6. The cross-reference does not fit the paragraph invoked.
"A well shall be deemed commenced when preparations for drilling have been commenced" leaves "preparations for drilling" undefined, so the triggering act is unbounded.

Addendum paragraph 16 defines commencement of operations as entry with equipment to build access roads followed by a drilling rig for spudding, a narrower test, and the Addendum priority clause makes the Addendum prevail. The two definitions do not sit together.

The royalty is one-eighth of "the price paid to Lessee" per thousand cubic feet, followed by struck-through language that would have allowed deduction of post-production costs for gathering, transportation, dehydration, extraction and compression; whether striking that language bars such deductions, or merely leaves the point silent, is the central ambiguity. "The price paid to Lessee" also fixes neither the point of sale nor the arm's-length character of the sale.

Subparagraph (A) promises oil royalty "free of cost" while subparagraph (C) directs the Lessee to deduct the Lessor's share of severance and other taxes from the (A) and (B) payments, so the lease elsewhere both forbids and mandates deductions from royalty. That tension bears directly on whether post-production costs may be netted.

The clause fixes a shut-in payment but never says it maintains the lease, a gap that must be read against paragraph 2's habendum requiring production in paying quantities or capability of production. Whether shut-in payments hold the lease past the primary term is unresolved.

This paragraph reserves "the further right of drilling or not drilling ... as the Lessee may elect," while paragraph 8 states the Lessee "shall be required to maintain a well density of at least 1 well per 160 acres" in a unit. The unfettered election and the mandatory density cannot both stand unqualified.

"Lessee shall be required to maintain a well density of at least 1 well per 160 acres contained in such unit" is susceptible of being read as an affirmative obligation to drill one well for every 160 acres, or merely as a constraint on how a unit may be formed; "maintain" fixes no date by which the density must be achieved, and "such unit" takes its content from the pooling sentence it was lifted from. Each reading yields a different result on breach.

Read as a drilling obligation the sentence contradicts paragraph 7, which reserves to the Lessee the right "of drilling or not drilling on the leased premises ... as the Lessee may elect," and paragraph 20, which forbids reading any implied covenant or obligation into the lease. Harmonising all three is precisely what a court would be asked to do.

The Lessor's waiver of "notice of any assignment or transfer of the within lease" conflicts with Addendum paragraph 17, which obliges the Lessee to give written notice of any assignment of a 51% or greater interest within fourteen days. The Addendum is stated to prevail over inconsistent main-body terms.

"Any damages if not mutually agreed upon" go to three appraisers and "Arbitration shall be mandatory," but the paragraph enumerates only crop and drainage damages, leaving the catch-all's reach and the enforceability of the appraisal as an arbitration undefined.

The Lessor must abide by "all reasonable safety policies of Lessee ... including but not limited to" one enumerated setback, so the catch-all's reach beyond that single specific is undefined and is set unilaterally by the Lessee.

The surrender clause reduces "the land rental hereinbefore set forth" in proportion to the acreage surrendered, but paragraph 3 makes this a "paid up bonus lease" and the instrument sets forth no land rental. The reduction mechanism has no referent.

"Force majeure, including but not limited to acts of God, strikes, riots and governmental restrictions" leaves the catch-all's reach beyond the enumerated events undefined, and it is unclear whether the lease is extended only for ninety days after the event ends.

The Lessee need only "meet or commence to meet all or any part of the breaches alleged" within thirty days, which does not say what discharges this condition precedent to suit. Whether beginning to address part of a breach suffices is open.

The extension payment is to be tendered "in the same manner as provided in Paragraph numbered 6 hereof with regard to the method of payment of shut-in royalties," but paragraph 6 fixes the shut-in rate while paragraph 5 prescribes the method of payment. The cross-reference points at the wrong paragraph.

The bar on reading any "implied covenant, agreement or obligation" into the lease has to be reconciled with paragraph 8's express requirement that the Lessee maintain a well density of one well per 160 acres, and with the Addendum incorporated by paragraph 26 which supersedes inconsistent main-body terms. The scope of the disclaimer is a live question.

This paragraph and Addendum paragraph 13 address Clean and Green liability in different terms, the Addendum adding CREP and limiting the trigger to operations on the Lessor's lands. Which text governs falls to the Addendum priority clause.

Locations are to be fixed by "mutual consent" with the Lessor's consent not unreasonably withheld, whereas Addendum paragraph 3 deems approval given if the Lessor does not return the approval form within thirty days. The two consent regimes differ.

The undertaking not to assert a right to transport gas from other lands unless the premises are pooled contradicts paragraph 1, which grants that transport right "regardless of the source of such production" and makes it survive the term; Addendum paragraph 20 states the prohibition without the pooling exception.

The clause bites only on an "inconsistency" with the main body, and the instrument supplies several candidates — Addendum paragraph 20 against paragraph 1's transport grant, Addendum paragraph 21 against the lease of coalbed methane, Addendum paragraph 17 against paragraph 11's notice waiver. Determining inconsistency is itself the construction exercise.

Restoration "as nearly as possible" to the pre-drilling condition "within 90 days, weather permitting" states neither a measurable standard nor a firm deadline. Both are open-ended on the face of the clause.

"As near its original condition as is reasonably possible" is a differently worded and looser standard than Addendum paragraph 1's "as nearly as possible," and it carries no deadline. Which standard governs the same restoration work is unclear.

Deemed approval through thirty days' silence is hard to reconcile with main-body paragraph 23, which requires drilling sites, roads and pipelines to be located by "mutual consent" of Lessor and Lessee. Whether silence can supply that consent would have to be decided.

The indemnity runs to "any and all claims, liens, damage or expense ... of whatsoever kind ... arising out of or caused by any actions or omissions of the Lessee," a catch-all appended to the specific penalty-for-violation-of-law promise, so its outer limit is undefined. There is no carve-out for the Lessor's own conduct.

The covenant that the Lessee acquires no right to drill an underground gas or oil storage well conflicts with paragraph 1's grant of the right of "injecting and storing, air, gas, brine and other substances from any source and into any subsurface strata." The line between the two is genuinely contestable.

The trigger is a "material adverse change in the quality of Lessor's water supply" "during or immediately after the completion" of drilling; neither the materiality threshold nor the window is defined. Both would have to be construed before the clause could be applied.

This paragraph and main-body paragraph 21 govern the same Clean and Green liability in different terms, the Addendum adding CREP and confining the trigger to operations on the Lessor's lands. Which controls turns on the Addendum priority clause.

The election to take "a 'cash equivalency' payment times the annualized wellhead price" in lieu of an allotment of 300,000 cubic feet of gas does not yield a computable sum, since a payment multiplied by a price states no amount. The value of the elected alternative cannot be derived from the words.

The clause commutes a free-gas "allotment of three hundred thousand cubic feet" that no other provision of the lease grants; the only free-gas right in the instrument is paragraph 8's gas for one dwelling house on a unit owner's land. The entitlement being converted has no source in the rest of the lease.

This definition of commencement conflicts with main-body paragraph 3, under which a well is "deemed commenced when preparations for drilling have been commenced"; the Addendum requires equipment, access-road construction and a rig for spudding. The two tests are not interchangeable.

The duty to give written notice of an assignment of a 51% or greater interest conflicts with main-body paragraph 11, under which the Lessor "waives notice of any assignment or transfer of the within lease." Whether notice is due depends on which provision governs.

The fee is payable "upon commencement of drilling operations," a trigger the instrument defines twice and differently — Addendum paragraph 16 versus main-body paragraph 3's "preparations for drilling." When the fee falls due therefore depends on which definition applies.

"Foreign gas" is nowhere defined, and the clause simultaneously denies the right to transport it and confirms a right to transport gas "produced from the premises unitized herewith" — leaving unclear whether unitized third-party gas is foreign. The two sentences pull against each other.

The denial of any right to move foreign gas across the premises contradicts paragraph 1, which grants the right to transport production "from the subject and other lands ... regardless of the source," surviving the lease term, and it is stated more absolutely than paragraph 25's pooling exception.

The covenant that the Lessee "has not acquired and does not acquire the rights to develop and/or produce coalbed methane gas" without the Lessor's prior written consent cannot be squared with the main body, which leases coalbed methane gas in paragraph 1, measures the term by its production in paragraph 2 and fixes a royalty on it in paragraph 4(B). The Addendum priority clause makes the conflict live.
